mappings.note: The Kumbh sites and the amrita legend that sanctifies them - a religious tradition and the belief behind it. LO-150 is the frame's only outcome about religious ideas, and this chapter's sacred-geography content has no closer home.

Sacred trees, groves and hills matched to the communities that protect them. Filed under conservation sensitivity because the subject is protected flora and natural sites, not a religious movement's origin.
The keyed statement is that protected sacred groves harbour biodiversity - conservation of flora and fauna, stated almost in the outcome's own words.
A forest patch protected for a deity, with hunting and felling banned, has to be named a sacred grove. Community conservation of flora, so LO-146 rather than LO-150.
Names the Uttarapatha. Trade-route history, which no LO in this frame covers; the sacred-geography outcomes do not apply to a commercial road.
'Punyakshetra' as a holy territory. Religious vocabulary of sacred space; not LO-142, because nothing is located on a map.

The Suzuki passage asks what follows for our treatment of air, water, land, trees and mountains if we see them as sacred rather than as resources. That is conservation sensitivity in the outcome's own terms.
Investigating local sacred sites and the stories that make them sacred. Religious belief and practice, so LO-150.
Why rivers, mountains and forests are held sacred (LO-150) and how they sustain life and ecosystems (LO-146). The expected answer needs both halves.
Why pilgrims visit a tirtha - merit, purification, vows, inner peace. Religious motivation, so LO-150.
Pilgrimage routes feeding trade and sacred sites supporting regional economies. Economic history, which no LO covers; the religion outcome would miss the commercial argument.
Sacred places shaping festivals, rituals, art and community identity. Religious ideas working on culture, so LO-150 rather than the conservation lane.
A project on the significance of two chosen sacred sites. Religious significance is what the task asks for.
The twofold significance of a tirthayatra - outward journey and inward transformation. Religious practice, so LO-150.
Defines sacredness as deep religious or spiritual value. The conceptual anchor of the chapter, and squarely a religious idea.
Bhudevi as Mother Earth - a religious personification of the planet. Not LO-146: the item asks for the term, not for any act of conservation.
The Char Dham placed at the four corners as a sacred circumambulation of the land. A pilgrimage system; LO-142 would be wrong because the outcome concerns climatic regions, not shrines.
Matches jyotirlingas, Shakti pithas, Char Dham and takhts to their traditions, keyed on Sikhism. Religious traditions and their sacred networks.
The Shakti Pitha legend read as sanctifying the whole land as the goddess's body. Interpretation of a religious idea, so LO-150.
The Nadistuti Sukta as a Vedic hymn praising rivers. A religious text; not LO-151, which is specifically about bhakti and sufi poetry and the social order.
Defines 'sangam' as the confluence of rivers - a physical feature, which the identify-and-describe-landforms competency covers. The sacred framing is context; the answer is geographical.
Locates the Ajmer dargah of Moinuddin Chishti, a shrine drawing people of many faiths. A sacred site of the sufi tradition, so LO-150; not LO-149, because the tomb's architecture is not discussed.
Why sites tied to the Buddha's life are sacred in Buddhism. The logic by which a religious tradition makes a place holy.
Defines a relic as the remains or belonging of a venerated figure. Religious vocabulary under LO-150.
Places the Akal Takht within the Golden Temple complex. A sacred-site recall of the Sikh tradition; the item asks where it is, not how it was built, so not LO-149.
Defines tirthayatra as pilgrimage. Religious practice, the central concept of the chapter.
Millennia of pilgrimage making the whole subcontinent sacred. The chapter's core religious idea, so LO-150 rather than a geography outcome.
Tirthankaras as the supreme preachers of dharma in Jainism. Doctrine of a religious tradition.
The Pandharpur wari of the Varkaris in Maharashtra - a living pilgrimage tradition. Not LO-151, because no poetry is quoted or interpreted.
Converging pilgrim and trade routes carrying goods and ideas between regions. Economic and cultural history, so the history goal rather than the religion outcome.
Sorts the real reasons mountains are revered - height as a threshold, links to deities, the journey itself - from easy access. Religious idea, so LO-150.
Granting a mountain legal personhood to honour an indigenous worldview is protection of a natural feature. Conservation sensitivity carries the answer, so LO-146 rather than LO-150.
Puri as the eastern Char Dham site. A pilgrimage-circuit recall; LO-142 concerns climatic regions, not shrines.
'Tirtha' as a river ford and, by extension, a place of spiritual crossing. The etymology is given to explain the religious idea, so LO-150 rather than the landform competency.
Contrasts the universal sacredness of Bhudevi with the particular sanctity of Haridwar. A distinction between two religious conceptions of sacred space.
Matches sacred sites to the traditions that revere them, keyed on Niyam Dongar and the Dongria Kondh. Religious traditions across faiths.
Religious protection of groves leading to biodiversity and water conservation - the reason statement is the conservation outcome itself. Not LO-150, because the payoff being tested is ecological.
Regional names for sacred groves - kavu, devarai, oran - across India. Kept with the other sacred-grove items under conservation of flora.
Statements on the Kumbh cycle, the Peepul across faiths and Jain tirthas linked to Tirthankaras' liberation. Religious traditions throughout.
A journey to four shrines in the four directions has to be identified as the Char Dham Yatra. A pilgrimage-tradition item, like the other Char Dham questions.
